kernelIdea: Tracing proofs backwards must terminate. Axioms are the statements taken as true without proof; a mathematical theory is its axioms plus everything derivable from them.

kernels.l1: Keep asking why until you reach something everybody just agrees on. That is where you start.
kernels.l2: Every reason leans on an earlier reason, but the chain has to stop somewhere. The things we agree on at the start are the rules of the game, and changing them gives a different game.
kernels.l3: Every proof rests on earlier facts, and tracing back must stop somewhere. The statements we agree to accept without proof are axioms, and a different choice of axioms gives a different mathematics.
kernels.l4: Tracing any proof backwards must terminate, so some statements are taken as true without proof. Those are axioms, and a theory is its axioms together with everything derivable from them.
kernels.l5: Axioms are chosen, not discovered; a good system is small, independent, consistent, and strong enough to produce what you want.
kernels.l6: Changing the axioms changes the mathematics — dropping the parallel postulate gives geometries as consistent as Euclid’s.
kernels.l7: Because the backward chain of justification must terminate, some statements are accepted without proof; these axioms are chosen, and the criteria are independence, consistency, and adequacy.
kernels.l8: Axioms are where the chain of *why* stops, not truths too obvious to argue with. They are judged by consistency and independence, and Gödel showed that settling every question is not on offer.
